paragraphs: Good, love, and benevolence are inherently relational—none can exist in isolation, for each requires another to be given and received; as Buber observes, the self becomes fully itself only in relation to a Thou [45]. Humanity inherits two such yearnings: a yearning for relationship, rooted in the creator’s own need for relationship to fulfill and overflow, and a yearning for oneness, rooted in the original unity from which creator and creation sprang and toward which both now return.

This yearning unfolds first toward the creator, the bond that gives existence its deepest meaning, and then toward fellow human beings, since all creation shares the same source—so to relate to another is to relate to the creator reflected within them. The Ten Commandments embody this order directly: the first four bind humanity to the creator, the remaining six to one another [39]; Jesus later distills this structure into a single summary—love the creator with all one’s heart, and love one’s neighbor as oneself [40].

The same root drives humanity further, toward ever-wider circles of oneness: the Confucian vision of Da Tong, the Great Unity, imagines the whole world as one family under Heaven [43]. Aristotle observes that household, village, and polis form a natural ascent toward the common good [16], while the Confucian Great Learning traces a parallel flow—goodness overflowing from the creator through the self, outward to family, community, and nation [47]. Kabbalah names the deeper aim beneath both: scattered divine sparks are gathered back into unity through ever-widening circles of righteous action [50]—each circle a small enactment of the larger oneness creation itself was made for.

Two traditions converge on this same oneness, naming it as humanity’s very mission: to make the world a welcoming dwelling place for the divine. In Jewish thought, this is Immanuel—God with us—the creator’s own spirit placed within creation [46]. In Chinese thought, this is Tian Ren He Yi, the oneness of Heaven and humanity, pursued through the Great Learning until mind, body, family, community, and nation each become a fit dwelling for Heaven [47]. East and West thus name the same mission of humanity: to make the self, and every circle it belongs to, a home for the creator to extend its presence.
